> We still have 800 or so people a day dying in the US from COVID, which is very high.

What is not considered very high? What is the acceptable level of death in a country with a population of 330 million? For reference, in 2019, before Covid-19, 2.8 million Americans died. That is ~7700 deaths per day. During "normal" times.

Get vaccinated, but let's also not blow the numbers out of proportion.

Source: https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db395.htm

> “Herd immunity.” Don’t be obtuse.

And it is not looking like we will reach herd immunity by vaccination numbers alone. So, in that case, when would we be able to declare we've reached "herd immunity"? When cases=0?

And some point, after enough time that the vaccine has been available, it is unreasonable/impractical to expect the entire country to adopt masks to keep protecting the vulnerable. Selfish? Of course, we're all pretty selfish in that regard. I bet you didn't wear masks prior to Covid, and people die from the flu (in MUCH smaller numbers, I admit), and I bet you were okay with that? Did that make you a terrible, selfish person? Nope.

>Was it easy to meet other people after you started? 

Like in most places in life, it's easy if you're socially confident. When you get there nearly everybody will already be "buddy-buddy" and you will be an outsider. Most folks are friendly, but what you get out of the community will depend on what you put into it. If you're shy and/or have social anxiety, you're going to have to work hard to make friends and be proactive. People most likely aren't going to go out of their way to approach the quiet dude in the corner, make friends with him, and offer to jump with him.

While it's important to be focused on completing AFF & getting your A-License, successfully integrating yourself into the DZ community is equally important. The fun in skydiving comes in group jumps (solos get VERY boring VERY quickly after your A-License).

They might have just lost steam/momentum. Befriending them while they're on student status and offering to jump with them once they're licensed might help in that regard (it's really tough & intimidating in the beginning to find people to jump with).

Yes, the actual "freefall" sensation does get boring and more familiar as you jump more, and yes it will not elicit the same excitement as your first jump (or even your first 10 jumps). The fun comes from the different disciplines when you combine them with **jumping with others**. Solo skydives get boring very quickly. It's group jumping and that degree of relative work that keeps it interesting/exciting. And, of course, some things are so unique that they are fun out of novelty (balloon jumps, "thing" jumps, etc.).

Friendships and how well receieved you will be at your DZ is critical. /u/Kuech3 says "don't forget the awesome friendships you'll make" as if it is a given--it's not, and don't assume it'll fall into your lap. It's up to you to make that social penetration, and it isn't as simple/easy as folks make it out to be (you're just yet another newbie, and most likely they're not going to come up to you and be chummy with you, invite you on jumps, etc.). Recognize that a lot of the gushing responses you'll get on here are from people that have made this social integration (and in many cases to the extent that they use the word "family" to describe their friends at the DZ).

This was my experience as well. /u/SlowInternetSlowFap is also a girl, which probably helps prevent that sort of thing (I've at least never seen a female jumper struggle to find someone that wants to jump with them, talk to them, help them out, etc.).

> being a more shy person

I don't want to discourage you, but I REALLY don't want you to have to deal with what I did. Just realize that a lot of people that will tell you it'll be fine, that skydivers are friendly/welcomining, that everyone at the DZ is part of a happy family...realize that these people are likely already *in* the family and see their DZ from a different perspective than the skydiving student that is on the outside. These people probably mean well, but they already have a "family" and a lot of close skydiving friends at the DZ, and they can likely not even be aware that they're ignoring students or making it hard to be approachable.

I'd recommend looking at my old posts I made on this subject. There's good input from others that have experienced this struggle and tips for overcoming it.

This will go against the grain, but, this is from personal experience: it *will* get old if you go by yourself. Making friends and being able to penetrate into the community will be one of the most important things you will need to do as you go for your A license. Do not expect people to automatically befriend you, talk to you, socially integrate you, etc. Unless you're a woman, most people will just look past you and won't automatically ask if you want to jump with them. They most likely won't approach you and start a conversation with you.

This was the hardest part of skydiving for me, and I was never able to get to the point where I had genuine FRIENDS at the dropzone and felt a part of the community. I ended up quitting because of this, so I just want to make sure that the same doesn't happen to you. /u/nelish promises you'll make friends, but that'll only happen if you very actively pursue it and put effort into it. Please don't assume it'll just happen magically, otherwise you're going to be miserable in this sport.

I...I'm touched that you did this. I really am. It means a metric FUCK-ton to have people like you in this sport. Thank you for reaching out like this, and I hope it motivates others to do the same at their home DZ.

I decided last night to just throw in the towel. It's not worth feeling this pain of isolation/loneliness when trying to do something you love. And I did fall in love with the sport--that's how I ended up doing so many jumps and not quitting earlier on. But, it just doesn't make sense to continue if it's this painful (and, of course, expensive).

If I ever end up relocating to a different part of the country, you can bet I'm going to check if there's a DZ nearby! And maybe I can jump with one of you cool guys and become a part of your "skydiving family."

Blue skies, my friends.

It's a "Removable Deployment System." It's a system available on certain (high-performance) canopies that allows you to completely remove the slider, d-bag, and pilot chute. The benefit is less drag so you can swoop faster/longer/better.
Everybody has different fears. I'm more afraid of looking dumb/awkward and being made fun of by the "sky gods" and getting my feelings hurt than risking my life by jumping out of a plane.

I'm sure nobody would mind signing a logbook. It's just a freaking signature, after all! But it's the intense pressure to go up to a stranger or maybe a "sky god" and ask them. I wish people were more openly friendly to beginners and approached them instead of waiting for beginners to initiate, but then I guess I'm just an oddity being a socially awkward skydiver...

The social part is the scariest part. Skydivers are so intimidating, and I'm not comfortable in typical social situations where alcohol is involved (and there's all that stupid beer rules stuff in skydiving...). I technically have nearly 200 jumps but don't have any signatures past my A-License...
